newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Disney's Shamrock eyes Israeli privatisations.
newsitem.headline: Disney's Shamrock eyes Israeli privatisations.

text.p: Shamrock Holdings Inc, a U.S. company that has invested heavily in Israel in recent years, is now eyeing stakes in privatised companies, its president Stanley Gold said on Sunday.

"We would like to be an active participant in certain of the privatisations that this government says are just around the corner," he told the international Jerusalem Business Conference that opened on Saturday night.

Gold told Reuters that Shamrock would consider co-investing with Koor Industries Ltd, in which it has a 22.5 percent stake. But, he said, Shamrock was also prepared to buy privatised companies on it own.
He would not say which companies or sectors interested Shamrock, the investment company for the family of Roy Disney.

The Israeli government is expected to announce a wide-ranging privatisation programme later this month. Besides Koor, by far its biggest Israeli holding, Shamrock has invested in two Israeli media companies and an energy concern.

Jonathan Solomon, executive director of strategy and business development for Britain's Cable & Wireless Plc, denied his company sought to take control of Bezeq Israel Telecom, the state-controlled phone company.

"Cable & Wireless would like to increase its holding in Bezeq," he said. "This is not to say Cable & Wireless wants to take over Bezeq or control it...Cable and Wireless would simply like to work in partnership with Bezeq."

The U.K. company acquired 10 percent of Bezeq in 1995. C&W has since been at odds with the government over the company's future role with Bezeq. According to Israel's Communications Ministry it has told the government its wants to raise its holding to 21 percent.
Gold, meanwhile, defended continued foreign investment in the Israeli economy despite doubts about the future of Middle East peace since the election of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in May.
"You cannot have a growing economy at least without the makings of peace," he said. "(But) we think perceptions will change, so get in early."
Gold expressed more concern about Israeli exchange rates. He estimated that what he termed the "overvalued" shekel was costing Koor $40 million to 50 million in annual earnings.
